questions.text: What distinguishes a monopoly from a price-taking firm?

options.a: A monopoly takes a perfectly elastic market price as given.
options.b: A monopoly faces market demand and chooses output with an effect on its selling price.
options.c: A monopoly is a buyer of labor only.
options.d: A monopoly necessarily produces without any costs.

questions.text: What is the profit-maximizing interior condition for a monopolist?

options.a: Total revenue equals total fixed cost.
options.b: Price equals average fixed cost.
options.c: Marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
options.d: Price equals marginal revenue at every output.

questions.text: For a downward-sloping inverse demand P(y), how does marginal revenue compare with price for positive output?

options.a: Marginal revenue equals average fixed cost.
options.b: Marginal revenue is below price.
options.c: Marginal revenue always exceeds price.
options.d: Marginal revenue equals price at every output.

questions.text: Why is monopoly marginal revenue below price?

options.a: Increasing sales generally requires lowering price on units sold as well as the marginal unit.
options.b: Price must increase to sell more units.
options.c: A monopolist is a price taker.
options.d: Marginal revenue equals marginal cost by definition at every quantity.

questions.text: For linear inverse demand P(y)=a-by, what is marginal revenue?

options.a: a-by.
options.b: a+by.
options.c: a-2b.
options.d: a-2by.

questions.text: At what region of a standard downward-sloping demand curve does a profit-maximizing monopolist with nonnegative MC operate?

options.a: An elastic region, with absolute elasticity greater than one.
options.b: Only where demand is vertical.
options.c: Only at a point of zero demand.
options.d: An inelastic region with negative MR.

questions.text: Why is operating on an inelastic region inconsistent with profit maximization when MC is nonnegative?

options.a: Fixed cost must exceed revenue.
options.b: Marginal revenue is positive in the inelastic region.
options.c: Increasing output raises price.
options.d: Reducing output raises revenue and weakly reduces cost.

questions.text: What happens to a monopolist's markup when demand is more elastic, holding marginal cost fixed and positive in the standard constant-elasticity case?

options.a: The markup does not depend on elasticity.
options.b: The markup becomes infinite.
options.c: The optimal markup rises.
options.d: The optimal markup over marginal cost falls.

questions.text: How is the Lerner index (P-MC)/P related to the absolute demand elasticity at a monopoly interior optimum?

options.a: It equals 1/absolute elasticity.
options.b: It equals marginal cost divided by quantity.
options.c: It equals 1 + absolute elasticity.
options.d: It equals absolute elasticity.

questions.text: In the competitive limit of infinitely elastic demand facing the firm, what happens to the monopoly markup condition?

options.a: Price becomes twice marginal cost.
options.b: Price approaches marginal cost.
options.c: Price approaches zero regardless of cost.
options.d: Marginal revenue becomes negative.

questions.text: For a monopolist with linear demand, how does MR compare graphically with inverse demand?

options.a: It is a horizontal line at zero price.
options.b: It has the same slope but twice the intercept.
options.c: It lies strictly above demand at all quantities.
options.d: It shares the vertical intercept but is twice as steep downward.

questions.text: Why may monopoly output be lower than efficient competitive output?

options.a: Monopoly always has lower marginal costs.
options.b: The monopolist restricts quantity until marginal revenue rather than price equals marginal cost.
options.c: The monopolist must set price equal to marginal cost.
options.d: Consumers cannot purchase any good at a monopoly.

questions.text: What is a factor's marginal revenue product (MRP)?

options.a: The additional revenue generated by employing one more unit of the factor.
options.b: The average profit earned by all firms.
options.c: Total revenue divided by total wages.
options.d: The factor's marginal physical product alone.

questions.text: If the factor affects output through y=f(x), which relationship holds for a monopoly producer?

options.a: MRP_x = MP_x divided by MR_y.
options.b: MRP_x = total revenue plus factor price.
options.c: MRP_x = MR_y times MP_x.
options.d: MRP_x = P times total output.

questions.text: For a competitive seller, what is the marginal revenue product of an input?

options.a: Market output minus fixed cost.
options.b: Marginal cost multiplied by wage.
options.c: The factor's average product divided by output price.
options.d: Output price multiplied by its marginal product.

questions.text: Why is the marginal revenue product of a factor generally less under monopoly than under price-taking output behavior at a given output and factor use?

options.a: Monopoly marginal revenue is less than output price.
options.b: Monopoly factor wages are always zero.
options.c: Monopoly physical marginal product must be lower.
options.d: Monopoly faces a perfectly elastic output demand.

questions.text: If both firms face a common factor wage and comparable technology, which factor-demand pattern arises in the standard model?

options.a: The monopolist always hires more.
options.b: Both necessarily hire identical quantities at all wages.
options.c: A monopoly output seller hires less of the factor than an otherwise comparable competitive seller.
options.d: A monopoly always hires zero workers.

questions.text: What is the factor-hiring condition for a monopoly output seller that buys labor competitively?

options.a: Wage equals total revenue.
options.b: Average product equals the wage.
options.c: MRP of labor equals the market wage.
options.d: Price times output equals the wage.

questions.text: What is the factor-hiring condition for a competitive output seller that buys labor competitively?

options.a: Market wage equals market output demand.
options.b: Value of marginal product equals the market wage.
options.c: Wage equals total fixed cost.
options.d: Marginal revenue product must be negative.

questions.text: What is a monopsony?

options.a: A market with many price-taking employers.
options.b: A market with one seller.
options.c: A market with perfect competition on both sides.
options.d: A market with a single buyer, such as one dominant employer of a particular factor.

questions.text: What type of factor supply curve does a simple monopsonist typically face?

options.a: Perfectly horizontal at every price.
options.b: Upward sloping.
options.c: A vertical demand curve.
options.d: Downward sloping because wages fall with hiring.

questions.text: Why can the marginal expenditure on labor exceed the wage paid by a monopsonist?

options.a: Marginal product of labor is necessarily negative.
options.b: Hiring an additional worker may require raising the wage on previously employed workers too.
options.c: The firm sells output at a higher price.
options.d: Labor supply must be perfectly elastic.

questions.text: If inverse labor supply is w(L)=a+bL for b positive, what is marginal labor expenditure?

options.a: a+bL.
options.b: a+2bL.
options.c: a-bL.
options.d: 2a+bL.

questions.text: What is the usual interior hiring condition for a monopsonist that is competitive in its output market?

options.a: Value of marginal product equals marginal factor expenditure.
options.b: Wage equals marginal product divided by output price.
options.c: Marginal factor expenditure equals zero.
options.d: Wage equals total labor cost.

questions.text: How does the monopsony wage compare with the marginal expenditure on labor at positive employment under increasing factor supply?

options.a: Wage always equals marginal labor expenditure.
options.b: Wage is lower than marginal labor expenditure.
options.c: Wage is higher than marginal labor expenditure.
options.d: Marginal expenditure must be negative.

questions.text: Relative to a competitive labor market with the same supply and labor demand schedules, monopsony generally leads to what?

options.a: Identical wages and employment.
options.b: Higher wages and lower employment necessarily.
options.c: Lower wages and lower employment.
options.d: Higher wages and higher employment.

questions.text: Why is monopsony employment Pareto inefficient in the standard model?

options.a: Labor supply becomes perfectly elastic.
options.b: Every employed worker is paid more than marginal revenue product.
options.c: Workers whose value of marginal product exceeds their opportunity cost are not hired.
options.d: The firm hires until wage equals product price at every quantity.

questions.text: What is the elasticity-adjusted wage bill condition for a monopsonist, with positive factor supply elasticity eta?

options.a: Marginal factor expenditure equals wage times (1+1/eta).
options.b: Marginal expenditure always equals wage.
options.c: Wage equals output price times eta.
options.d: Marginal factor expenditure equals wage times (1-1/eta).

questions.text: What happens to the monopsony wedge between wage and marginal expenditure as labor supply becomes very elastic?

options.a: It becomes smaller.
options.b: It turns negative.
options.c: It becomes infinite even when supply is perfectly elastic.
options.d: It necessarily becomes larger.

questions.text: In the standard competitive labor market, a binding minimum wage above equilibrium generally does what?

options.a: Reduces employment demanded relative to the competitive level.
options.b: Increases labor demand at all wage levels.
options.c: Raises employment above the competitive level without exception.
options.d: Leaves employment unchanged at every minimum wage.

questions.text: Under monopsony, what may a suitably chosen minimum wage do?

options.a: Increase both the wage and employment relative to the unregulated monopsony outcome.
options.b: Eliminate the underlying labor supply curve.
options.c: Always decrease employment regardless of its level.
options.d: Necessarily leave employment unchanged.

questions.text: Why can a minimum wage increase employment in a monopsonistic labor market?

options.a: It must lower workers' reservation wages to zero.
options.b: It makes output demand perfectly elastic automatically.
options.c: Over a range of hiring, the employer can acquire workers at a fixed regulated wage rather than raise all incumbents' wages.
options.d: It shifts the marginal product curve to infinity.

questions.text: Why may a sufficiently high minimum wage reduce employment even in a monopsony market?

options.a: Firms can hire limitless labor at any regulated wage.
options.b: The labor supply curve becomes vertical at all wages.
options.c: All minimum wages necessarily improve employment forever.
options.d: Labor demand is downward sloping, and a wage above the relevant marginal value product discourages hiring.

questions.text: What is an upstream monopolist in a vertical supply chain?

options.a: A firm that supplies labor to households.
options.b: A monopolist selling an input used by another firm to produce a downstream good.
options.c: A monopolist selling directly to final consumers only.
options.d: A buyer with perfect competition in the factor market.

questions.text: What is a downstream monopolist in the two-stage model?

options.a: A firm that buys no inputs.
options.b: A monopolist choosing the upstream input's technological marginal cost.
options.c: A monopolist using the upstream product as an input to sell a final good.
options.d: A price-taking manufacturer facing horizontal demand.

questions.text: What is double marginalization?

options.a: Two perfectly competitive sellers charging price equal to cost.
options.b: A single firm paying the same fixed cost twice.
options.c: Two successive monopolists each charge a markup, raising the final price and restricting output.
options.d: Two firms competing aggressively to lower prices.

questions.text: Why can vertical integration eliminate the simple double-markup problem?

options.a: Integration guarantees marginal cost is zero.
options.b: Integration removes the need to produce an intermediate input.
options.c: Integration makes consumer demand perfectly inelastic.
options.d: The integrated firm accounts for the upstream input's true marginal cost rather than an inflated internal transfer price.

questions.text: In the lecture's linear-demand vertical monopoly model, how does integrated output compare to output under separate upstream and downstream monopolies?

options.a: Integrated output must be zero.
options.b: Both produce identical output.
options.c: The integrated monopolist produces twice as much as the separated pair, given the model's assumptions.
options.d: The integrated monopolist produces half as much.

questions.text: Why might separate upstream and downstream monopolists jointly earn less profit than a vertically integrated monopolist?

options.a: Each applies a markup without internalizing the negative effect on the other's sales.
options.b: Integration always doubles production costs.
options.c: Separation eliminates every markup.
options.d: The upstream firm cannot influence input price.

questions.text: Compared with vertically integrated monopoly, double marginalization typically produces what in the linear benchmark?

options.a: Identical quantities but higher fixed costs only.
options.b: The competitive allocation automatically.
options.c: Higher output and lower final-good price.
options.d: Lower output and higher final-good price.

questions.text: What is the socially efficient benchmark in a no-externality monopoly market with constant marginal cost?

options.a: Produce until marginal revenue is zero regardless of cost.
options.b: Choose output where price equals average fixed cost.
options.c: Set price equal to maximum willingness to pay with zero quantity.
options.d: Produce until buyers' marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost.

questions.text: What is the key difference between monopoly power and monopsony power?

options.a: Monopsony always faces a downward-sloping supply curve.
options.b: Monopoly power arises only in labor markets.
options.c: Monopoly power concerns a seller of output; monopsony power concerns a buyer of an input.
options.d: Both necessarily refer to the same firm's price-setting output decision.

questions.text: In the monopsony diagram, why does marginal labor expenditure lie above inverse labor supply?

options.a: Wages decrease whenever labor is hired.
options.b: Hiring more workers requires paying a higher wage on existing units as well.
options.c: Labor is supplied at a fixed wage regardless of employment.
options.d: Marginal productivity must always exceed output price.
